en: Part I. (p.
379) Oṃ! Homage to the glorious Hevajra.
Homage to the glorious Vajraḍāka, the sovereign of the circle of ḍākinīs, who possesses the five wisdoms and the three bodies, and who is the protector of the world.
Salutations always to as many Vajra-Ḍākinīs as there are— those who have severed the bonds of conceptual thought and who engage in the welfare of the world.
It is stated in the *Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi* by the venerable Nūtanānaṅgavajra:
"That [reality] can never be apprehended through knowledge derived from hearing and so forth,
because it lacks the characteristics of prosody and is devoid of both the characterized and the characteristics."
For this very reason, the virtuous should always engage in service to a true guru;
for without that, the ultimate reality cannot be attained even in tens of millions of eons.
But when the jewel of reality has not been attained, success is never achieved at all;
for just as there can be no sprout from the absence of a seed in a perfectly pure and fertile field.
Whatever traditional teachings there are that teach the meaning of wisdom and means,
they are as marvelous as wish-fulfilling jewels, established in the state of non-conceptuality.
Having thus understood the teachers on the surface of the earth according to their true nature,
one should attend upon them with diligence for the sake of attaining the supreme realization of the self.
He by whose splendor the infinite bliss of a bodhisattva is attained is to be served by all the Buddhas throughout the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
Why, then, do those of evil intent approach that embodiment of compassion, who is affectionate without cause,
with hearts defiled by illusion?
Having firmly served the true Guru with improper honors and genuine respect,
and through offerings such as milk and worship, that which was desired was obtained.
But when the jewel of reality— the abode of all the qualities of a Buddha— is attained,
those who are cruel in their search for faults will not even ask for news of it.
Nevertheless, such evil-minded ones approach the Guru, who is like a vajra;
with their own wicked intentions, they bring harm upon themselves by their own actions.
They are free from conceptual construction regarding the abduction of the Guru’s consort and the wealth of the Three Jewels,
as well as regarding the rejection of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) by yogins.
Thus it was said by the illustrious Lord Vajra: "O great elements,
you who possess a sense of revulsion are always causes of terror for me in this regard."
Having quickly approached a teacher with the thought, "He will not favor me," the wicked take refuge with others, eager to speak of his faults.
Thinking, "How may we obtain the title of 'Yogācārya'?",
they engage in this alone and do not seek after Buddhahood.
Having somehow attained that knowledge, some do not honor their former teacher;
intoxicated with pride, they say, "We are the knowers," while others do not even say this.
And others, being enraged, said: "Take him, he has been surrendered!
I am no longer your disciple today, nor are you my teacher now."
How could there be accomplishment or even happiness in this very life for those whose minds deceive their gurus? They wander about, utterly deluded.
And those beings who are of such a kind, being turned away from the welfare of themselves and others,
have all been declared by Vajrasattva to be people born of evil.
For those who hate themselves, there is no destination other than hell;
performing terrible deeds, they are cooked with various sufferings of men.
Therefore, those who desire their own ultimate welfare should always honor the teacher— who bestows infinite fruit— with their whole being.
Having abandoned envy and avarice, as well as pride and egoism,
along with deceit, hypocrisy, and harshness, those who are resolved upon true awakening [should act].
With a mind as unshakable as that of Sadāprarudita through his conduct,
one should attend upon the Lord of the World, the Guru who bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
And with supreme devotion, three times a day, preceded by offerings and maṇḍalas, they should bow their heads at his feet, regardless of their own affairs.
Then, through the grace of the presence of the Guru,
the disciples attain the supreme reality without obstacle, with a mind awakened to the three times.
Having abandoned pride, deceit, and the entire veil of hypocrisy,
those heroes who, with faith, serve the Guru according to the tradition here, even when he is not present.
Having attained the supreme state, all those Victors, the Sugatas,
reached that treasure of the qualities of a Victor, that jewel of reality, by means of which they attained awakening.
It is also stated in the *Mahālakṣmīsādhana*:
"That which is of unmanifest form is established within all bodies.
The supreme reality is obtained from the mouth of the Guru; there is no doubt in this matter.
There is no one more venerable than the teacher in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile;
by his grace, the various accomplishments are attained by the Buddhas.
Likewise, it has been stated by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna in the *Svādhiṣṭhānakrama*:
"Abandoning all other worship, one should undertake the worship of the Guru;
for when he is satisfied, that supreme knowledge of the Omniscient One is obtained."
What merit has not been performed by him, or what austerity has not been practiced,
through the worship of Vajrasattva, the unsurpassed teacher?
Whatever is unsurpassed or even more distinguished,
that indeed should be given to the guru by one who desires that very thing to be inexhaustible.
"The teacher removes sin; the teacher removes fear;
the teacher carries one across to the further shore from the great terror of the ocean of suffering."
Furthermore, regarding the sequence of perfect awakening, it is said:
"The Blessed One, the self-arisen, is the sole presiding deity;
yet, because he bestows instruction, the Vajrācārya is superior to him."
It is said elsewhere as well:
"A Buddha made of wood, even if lacking the nature of ethical discipline, grants liberation after hundreds of thousands of lifetimes."
In this very life as well, the Guru bestows with reverence that happiness which is eternal.
Indrabhūtipāda has also said:
"The Guru is the Buddha, and he is indeed the Dharma and the Saṅgha;
for it is through his grace that the supreme reality, the excellent Triple Gem, is attained."
Likewise, the venerable Saraha says:
"The Guru has bestowed the nectar-like essence of instruction; it has not been drunk by those [who lack devotion]."
Just as those who were thirsty might die on the desert wasteland with a weapon [in hand].
That very [scripture] is studied, that very [scripture] is recited, and upon the arrival of the treatise, that very [scripture] is explained;
yet he who does not perceive it through his own vision beholds only the feet of the singular supreme teacher.
Therefore, if from this most terrible saṃsāra— which has infinite objects and is an ocean of the Māras that is difficult to ward off— there arise protectors who are like ships;
[are they not so?]
Why is this? Because these people, agitated and overwhelmed by the many serpents of their own conceptual nets, will fail to attain here that Buddhahood which is the sole abode of supreme bliss.
And in the Vajraḍāka Tantra:
"Those men who, out of great delusion, step over the shadow of the guru, his wife, his sandals, his seat, or his bed, carry the edge of a razor."
Even if well-instructed, when a disciple transgresses the command of the guru,
he shall become a cripple in this world and dwell in hell in the next world.
By practicing deceit and guile to manifest false devotion,
one is born as one afflicted by consumption, leprosy, and other great diseases, and undergoes rebirth in the hells and other such realms.
Thinking thus, the disciples who are devoted to their guru then attain vast accomplishment by fulfilling the command of the guru.
In the *Śrī Hevajra Tantra* (p.
"Even that disciple who has attained accomplishment is one who illuminates perfect gnosis."
One should pay homage to the Guru for the sake of accomplishment, as he is the cause for abandoning the Avīci hell.
And likewise, in another place,
the Sage has said: "Having carefully discerned his disciples by means of an infallible sign, the Guru should employ them according to what is appropriate."
A capable teacher, having understood the disposition of the disciple, is able to instruct him;
therefore, the disciple should be favored by him, for a fool does not deserve to be a disciple.
Whatever was previously beneficial for someone, that one should continue to practice for them;
for one who is repelled is in no way a fit vessel for the true Dharma.
One who seeks the truth must first declare that "everything exists";
later, for one who has understood the meaning and is free from attachment, there is solitude.
One who desires merit should not speak of emptiness in every respect;
for is it not the case that medicine administered at the wrong place becomes poison?
Moreover:
Emptiness, when wrongly perceived, destroys the person of dull intellect,
just as a snake poorly grasped or a spell incorrectly performed [brings ruin].
Moreover, another fool who, due to his inability to understand this, considers himself a scholar,
will go headfirst to the Avīci hell, his soul destroyed by his own rejection [of the teaching].
As it has been said:
"To some one is born as a disciple, and to another one is born as a teacher;
the knower of means disciplines ignorant beings through various skillful means."

But the unvirtuous must be compassionated with even greater effort. As it has been said: "Just as a mother’s distress becomes especially intense when her son is ill, so too is the compassion of Bodhisattvas especially directed toward those who are unvirtuous."
Independence for a disciple is never desired at any time. He said:
"Independence for a disciple is always not desired by all the Buddhas.
For the independent ascent of a blind man onto a mountain is not auspicious.
In the examination of scripture, its independence is not denied;
for the wise always proceed only after having examined [it].
Once one has engaged [with it], having understood its nature in this way, its future state [should be considered].
"The Victors have declared that one should thus be engaged in meditative cultivation."
Likewise, it was also said by the venerable Śākyamitra in the *Anuttarasandhi*:
"One who is deceitful in mind, lazy, a reviler of the guru,
and whose mind is puffed up with pride, thinking 'I have received initiation'..."
"Omniscience is not easily attained"— with such a thought, that wretched person of inferior mind perceives only the faults of the teacher and not his virtues.
Deprived of service, he would not desire the truth even if it were light; with anger, he would move from his seat at the words of praise.
Having seen his teacher in the assemblies, he would turn his face away.
Then he should offer a salutation to him while he is in private.
And thus, one should avoid a bad disciple ruined by his own wickedness— even if he be one's own legitimate son—
likewise a Vaiśya, a king, or an elder brother, if they are censured by the noble ones.
A hero would never indeed act in such a manner in his presence.
Endowed with auspicious qualities, possessed of wisdom, and joined with vigor, he regards his teachers with devotion as equal to a Buddha;
having realized the Dharma of the Victorious One, he is deeply serene in the teaching.
He becomes a worthy recipient here; one should show him favor.
Though he has studied many tantras and is highly proficient in the scriptures,
having served his gurus and received the instruction on reality;
Even one who is expert in the scriptures is not capable of accomplishing what is for his own welfare;
moreover, those scriptures serve merely as a cause for his own destruction.
Now, there may be one who is fortunate, having received the instruction on reality, yet is dull-witted and incapable of synthesizing the meaning; such a person,
having abandoned the intellect that has been formed through teaching, proceeds [further].
Even he who is devoid of excellence in speech incurs contempt.
One who has studied many tantras, possesses wisdom, knows the six parameters,
and is endowed with the perfections of learning, intelligence, fortitude, memory, and vigor;
one who has received the instruction on reality through service to the gurus.
For he is indeed empowered to expound the instruction of the King of Tantras.
Likewise, in the Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra:
"Fire is known by smoke, and water by the crane;
by signs, the lineage of the wise Bodhisattva is known."
"The wise man, seeing the true nature of reality, bestows grace upon the good disciple, whose body hair stands on end with joy like a lotus blooming from the waters of supreme serenity."
As it was said by the venerable master Candrakīrti:
"Even while still an ordinary person, upon hearing of emptiness,
one repeatedly attains inner joy."
With eyes streaming from the outpouring of faith,
he becomes one whose body is covered in bristling hair.
He who possesses the seed for the mind of perfect enlightenment and is a vessel for the instruction on reality—
to him the ultimate truth should be explained.
The qualities of that [cause] follow as its consequences.
That is to say:
having undertaken ethical discipline, one always abides by it.
He gives gifts and cultivates compassion;
he practices patience and dedicates that merit toward awakening,
indeed for the liberation of the world.
Such is the detailed exposition. And it is said here:
"The perfection of the welfare of others is considered the primary fruit of the Buddhas;
Buddhahood and the rest, being for that purpose, are called fruits [only] in a secondary sense."
And all this entire fruit is perfected only through the cultivation of the yoga of the non-dual Mahāmudrā.

As it is said in the *Āryaprajñāpāramitā*: "One who wishes to train even on the level of the Śrāvakas should hear this very Prajñāpāramitā... up to... one must attain yoga right here in this Prajñāpāramitā. Likewise for the level of the Pratyekabuddhas... up to... for the level of the Bodhisattvas as well," and so forth in detail.

The Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā herself—whose other name is Mahāmudrā—has as her intrinsic nature non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*); therefore, the Blessed One, whose essence is the Dharmakāya, is likewise of that very same nature as the Vajra of Bodhicitta. As it is said: "Prajñāpāramitā is gnosis; she is the Tathāgata.
If Prajñāpāramitā alone is established in all vehicles, how then can there be a distinction between the vehicles? He replies:
O Lord, because the realm of phenomena is without differentiation, there is no distinction of vehicles;
yet the three vehicles were taught by you for the sake of introducing sentient beings [to the path].

To you who are dull-witted, thinking "the world consisting of blue and so forth truly exists," and who are terrified by the profound method due to being possessed by the demonic seizure of grasping at phenomena—
This diverse world is declared to be nothing but consciousness alone,
devoid of the distinction between the grasped object and the grasping subject— for those of dull intellect.
"Having intellects purified by the cultivation of immeasurable and infinite successions of eons, they perceive [reality] as having the form of a city of Gandharvas, marked by the two truths."
It has also been said by the venerable Saraha:
"Consciousness, free from the grasped and the grasper, is ultimately real;
thus it is sung by those who have reached the further shore of the ocean of the Yogācāra doctrine."
Even that consciousness which is held to be ultimate by the wise is not accepted [as real],
because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, like a lotus in the sky.
The Madhyamikas know reality to be free from the four extremes: it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither.
The venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna also said:
"Never, anywhere, do any entities exist that have arisen from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause."

Therefore, because they are devoid of the four alternatives, entities are indeed unproduced, since production from self, from another, from both, or from neither is untenable. To explain: in the first case, if that [entity] were produced from itself, there would be no distinction whatsoever. Due to the absence of such a distinction, sprouts and the like could not arise even when a seed is produced. If it is argued that the seed itself transforms into the state of a sprout, we say no; for the sprout differs in its configuration, color, taste, potency, and maturation. If it is argued that this occurs through the abandonment of the previous state of being a seed, [we respond as follows:]

In that case, the sprout now is indeed something else. How can that be said? Even so it is said: "Oh, what skill the proponents of transformation (pariṇāmavādins) possess! They destroy themselves while producing [something] once their power has perished."
The venerable master Candrakīrti has also said:
"Furthermore, even the world does not accept the identity of these two."
Since one perceives the effect even when the cause has perished,

it is therefore not logically tenable— either from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*) or even from the perspective of the world (*lokataḥ*)— to postulate that an entity arises from itself.

But a second [cause] does not exist. In that case, there would be the absurd consequence of a rice sprout arising from a kodrava seed, because of the commonality of "otherness" (*paratva*). If it is argued that this occurs by virtue of the specific power within its own continuum, then the rice seed would lack the power for a rice sprout because it is "other. If it is asked how there can be such a thing as "otherness" within a single continuum, then there would be no distinction whatsoever between the seed and the sprout; due to the absence of such a distinction, they would be identical. Since there is no "otherness" in a single entity, there is an absence of production. It is said:
"If the other were to arise in dependence upon something else, then thick darkness might arise from a flame."
Indeed, everything would arise from everything,
because the state of being "other" is equal in respect to every cause.
Therefore, "kārya" (the effect) is etymologically defined as that which can be produced (*śakyaṃ prakartum*);
for even a remote cause is so called because it is capable of its production,
and because [it is distinguished] from a producer that belongs to the same single continuum as the birth [of the effect].
And likewise, [the capacity] for the sprout of rice does not belong to *kodrava* and other such grains.
[Fragmentary text] ... [omitted] ... ... [omitted] ... ... [omitted] ...
...because of being other.
The sprout exists, yet it is certainly not simultaneous with the seed; how then could there be "otherness" without otherness?
Therefore, the birth of the sprout from the seed is not established.
Let the position that [the effect] arises from something else be abandoned.

The third [alternative], however, does not exist, because self-nature and other-nature are absolutely contradictory. For instance, the sprout, which is its own nature, is an unarisen entity; the seed, which is another nature, is an existent entity. How could it be from both? If it is argued that for that which is currently arising there is indeed an attainment of the other-nature—the seed—therefore there is production from itself in some respect and from another in some respect, and thus production certainly exists; we say no. Because that which is currently arising lacks existence. Only what is existent is "other. Otherwise, how could there be the designation "that which is arising"?

If this is so, what is the use of another seed? For that [seed] itself is unestablished. Therefore, that which is being born is unarisen because it does not exist; and that which is non-existent does not arise, just like the horn of a rabbit.

But the fourth [position] is deluded, because it entails the fault of causelessness. Furthermore, even the world does not perceive anything as being without a cause. He says: Those elements do not exist in the manner described—namely, that birth occurs generally from self, from another, or from both.
Furthermore, that which was previously refuted as being without cause— namely,
that these elements do not exist when they have not arisen— is therefore established.
Entities are devoid of intrinsic nature because they do not arise from themselves, from another, or from both, nor do they arise without depending on a cause;
for this reason, delusion is so abundant that it is like a dense mass of clouds.
Indeed, for you, the objects of the world do not appear falsely.

Just as someone, due to the influence of a visual disorder, perceives things that are unreal— such as hair, a second moon, a peacock’s tail-feathers, or flies— so too does the ignorant person, indeed, perceive through the fault of delusion.
For by means of the intellect, one indeed perceives the manifold conditioned world.
In this sequence, just as there is the non-arising of the wheel of the knowable (*jñeyacakra*), so too is there the non-arising of the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*). If that is so, then:
And it has been stated by the Blessed One in various sūtras:
"No external object exists in the way that it is conceptualized by the foolish;
rather, the mind, stirred by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), proceeds appearing as an object."
Likewise: for that Bodhisattva who dwells in wisdom has realized the reality that is dependent upon consciousness-only.
Seeing no subject of grasping apart from the object of grasping,
one realizes that the triple world is consciousness-only.
Just as waves arise from the great ocean through the impulsion of the wind,
so too [do they arise] from that which is called the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the seed of all.
It becomes mere consciousness through its own power.
Therefore, the dependent nature exists;
however, it is the basis for the establishment of designations,
as well as that which arises as an apprehended object even without an external [object].
The essential nature of the domain of all conceptual proliferation.
If it is argued that the mind exists even without anything external,
just as in a dream, then this very point must be considered:
for even in a dream, there is no such thing as "mind" for me.
When that is so, you have no illustrative example.
If there is a memory of the dream upon waking, then there must likewise be an external object;
for one remembers, "This was seen by me."
Just as in that case, there is likewise the occurrence of memory regarding external objects.
Since the very arising of visual cognition is established,
there is no such thing as a mental consciousness [distinct from it]; rather,
it is that very mind which is projected as having an external form.
If it is held that it is just as it is in a dream, so it is here as well.
Just as that external object was not produced for you, so too the mind was not produced in the dream;
nor were the eye and the objects of the eye, nor that which arises from them.
And all form, as well as the triad [of the senses, objects, and consciousness], is false.
Furthermore: if form itself has been negated therein,
having realized that "this is mind-only."
He spoke of that which is born of the karma of delusion; why then has this Great-Souled One returned here once more?
The mind alone constructs the world of sentient beings and the world of the environment in all their manifold variety;
for it has been taught that the entire universe arises from karma.
And having shaken off karma and mind, it does not exist.
How then was it stated by the Blessed One: "O sons of the Conqueror, the triple world is mind-only"? He replied:
"This teaching is for the sake of one who does not understand such exceedingly profound categories of reality."
The ālaya exists, and the person itself exists; indeed,
these aggregates, as well as the elements, exist.
Even though he had abandoned the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the Buddha still taught "I" and "mine";
likewise, he [taught] all phenomena, even though they lack intrinsic nature (*tathāsvabhāva*).
He taught that "it exists" as a provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
Just as a physician administers medicine according to each patient's specific illness,
so indeed do the Buddhas teach "mind-only" to sentient beings.
The venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna also said:
"The Sage’s teaching that 'the entire world is mind-only' was for the purpose of removing the fear of the ignorant; it is not [to be taken] as the ultimate reality."
Likewise: "O Protector, at the turning of the wheel of Dharma, you have revealed that all phenomena are primordially peaceful, unarisen, and by their very nature in a state of nirvana."
Likewise: "The wise declare that the cessation of conceptual constructions is the fruit of inquiry."
Ordinary people [perceive] through conceptualization alone, whereas the yogi, not conceptualizing Buddhas, attains liberation.
Seeing a snake that has entered a hole in his own house, an elephant casts off all fear, thinking "there is no other elephant here," and even abandons his dread of the serpent.
Oh, how great indeed is the uprightness of another!
Furthermore: form is not the self, nor indeed is the self possessed of form.
The self is not in form, nor does form exist in the self; know all the aggregates in this same way. These twenty-four factors are held to be merely objects of one's own view.
These are those peaks that have arisen, situated upon the vast mountain of the view of a self-existent body;
their essence is split asunder by the vajra of the realization of selflessness.
But the mountain of vision suddenly undergoes dissolution.
It was also said by Saraha:
"All these things are devoid of a nature that is either one or many; thus, through the separation from attachment, the diligent practitioner attains the state of a yogi.
What is craving? Where is that craving? When sought through investigation, it is not found."
Upon reflection regarding the world of living beings, who indeed here shall die?
Who will be? Who has been? Who is a kinsman? To whom does anyone belong as a friend?
Everything is like space; let those like me accept this.
And thus the Master has said:
"The absence of intrinsic nature in form and so forth is considered external emptiness;
the absence of intrinsic nature in both is internal-external emptiness."
The venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna also said:
"Whatever has arisen in dependence upon this or that has not arisen by way of its own-being.
How can that which has not arisen by way of its own-being be called 'arisen'?"
Likewise: that which is born from conditions is indeed unborn.
Its very arising would [occur] from its own intrinsic nature;
that which is dependent on conditions is said to be empty.
He who understands emptiness is heedful.
And so says the venerable master Candrakīrti:
"For those who have gone outside the path of the venerable master Nāgārjuna, there is no means to attain liberation."
For they have fallen away from the path of conventional truth;
and due to that fall, there is no attainment of liberation.
Conventional truth is the means,
and ultimate truth is the goal;
he who indeed does not discern the distinction between these two—
Through false conceptualizations, he has gone upon a wrong path.
The venerable Śāntideva also said:
"The conventional and the ultimate—these are considered the two truths.
Reality is that which is beyond the scope of the intellect; the intellect is called the conventional."
By cultivating the impression of emptiness, the impression of existence is discarded;
and by practicing the thought that "nothing exists," even that [impression] is later abandoned.
At that time, no entity is found which could be conceived as "non-existent";
how then could a non-entity, being without a basis, appear before the mind?
When neither existence nor non-existence stands before the mind, then,
due to the absence of any other alternative, it becomes supportless and subsides.
Thus, in this way, no refutation is tenable against the position of emptiness;
therefore, emptiness must indeed be cultivated without any doubt.
Since fear arises from that thing which produces suffering,
and emptiness is the pacifier of suffering— how then can fear arise from it?
If there were some "I" from whom fear could arise, then fear would exist;
but if I myself do not exist at all, for whom will there be fear?
Liberation, however, results from the vision of emptiness because it consists in the complete realization of its meaning;
yet in the teaching (*pravacana*), there is indeed the instruction on emptiness itself.

Among these, that which is definitive (*nītārtha*) is the direct teaching of emptiness, while the other is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), intended for the purpose of leading others to enter into emptiness.

Therefore, even the instruction on the cultivation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) was taught by the Blessed One solely for the purpose of introducing [the practitioner] to the cultivation of the non-dual yoga of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is free from conceptual proliferation. And so it is said: "For the foremost practitioners of yoga, the union of wisdom and means is indeed cultivation; the cultivation of the union with the Great Seal is what is called [cultivation] by the Victors."
Now, what is this wisdom (*prajñā*), what is the means (*upāya*), and how are they cultivated—conjointly or separately? To this it is replied:
That which is the non-ground of all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and the non-domain of words;
That awareness of the mind is proclaimed as wisdom (prajñā).

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is indeed the realization of the non-proliferation (*niḥprapañcatā*) of all phenomena. What is this non-proliferation? It is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). But if emptiness itself is a proliferation, how can it be non-proliferation? Nothing at all is affirmed by the word "emptiness," because nothing whatsoever is affirmed by words. The function of all words consists solely in the negation of superimposition (*samāropa*).

Therefore, the teaching of emptiness illuminates the nature of reality within the mental continuum of those to be trained by means of demonstrating the exclusion of all superimpositions; it does not, however, establish emptiness as a positive entity, which would result in that very emptiness becoming a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Thus it has been said:
"The Victors have declared that emptiness is the relinquishing of all views."
But those for whom emptiness itself is a [clinging] view were declared by them to be incurable.
Likewise:
"Those who perceive intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, as well as existence and non-existence, do not perceive the reality in the Buddha's teaching."
It was said by the Blessed One himself: "And terms such as 'emptiness' are the exclusion of all superimpositions."
And so it is said in the treatise:
"Those of small intelligence who perceive existence and non-existence do not see the auspicious cessation of conceptual proliferation regarding all things."
And if nirvāṇa were an entity, nirvāṇa would be conditioned; for no entity whatsoever exists anywhere that is unconditioned. Thus it is said.

[Objection: Surely, by the negation of both "existence" and "non-existence," it would be established through implication that [the object] simply does not exist; for when two things are negated, nothing else remains. To this, it is replied:

This entire refutation certainly applies to those who maintain both extremes. However, for one who has rejected the doctrine of both extremes, all that depends upon them [is likewise rejected]. For indeed, when those who accept the doctrine of both extremes have their position negated as an absolute certainty, they inevitably fall into the other extreme. But for one who has rejected the doctrine of both extremes, since their acceptance consists in the cessation of superimposition (*samāropa*), how could this fault apply? This is trivial. As it is said in the *Laṅkāvatāra*:

“O son of good family, apart from body and mind, from where else could vocal sounds emerge? He replied, “Lord of the Kinnaras, there is no emergence of vocal sound that is separate from space. He said, “Therefore, by this method, O son of good family, it should be understood thus: whatever activities of vocal sound emerge, they all emerge from space; for vocal sounds have the nature of space. Through cessation, they proceed correctly with the nature of space. Therefore, all phenomena—whether expressed or unexpressed—do not abandon that very equality with the limit of space. "The method is also fourfold, as described by Bodhivajra, as described by Buddhavajra... and so forth.

For this very reason, wisdom (*prajñā*) is characterized by non-existence (*abhāva*), while means (*upāya*) is characterized by existence (*bhāva*). Thus it has been said: "Wisdom is characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and means is characterized by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, they are impelled by the application of wisdom and means.
Then, like a multi-faceted jewel, they act for the benefit of sentient beings;
therefore, it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
Thus, the two divisions are established as "means" (*upāya*) and [wisdom].
Now this is investigated: Can Buddhahood be attained through wisdom (*prajñā*) alone, or not? Or even through the sequence of means (*upāya*) alone? To this it is said:

Buddhahood is not attained by wisdom alone, nor by means alone; rather, if both of these—characterized as wisdom and means—are of the nature of equality, if these two are of non-different form, if they are of a single aspect—[then] enjoyment and liberation [are attained]. And so it has been said: "Then both are enjoyment and liberation."
Because it brings about the desired result quickly, like a boat,
through a state of constant favorable connection, it is proclaimed as "upāya" (the means).
And that which is the simultaneous opening of both, like water and milk,
through union with the non-dual form— that is called wisdom and means.
That which can neither be cast in nor removed,
and which remains even when that for the sake of which it was cast away has been abandoned— that is called reality (tattva) according to the Dharma.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, it remains forever for the entire world,
perfectly bestowing both enjoyment and liberation through its nature as wisdom and means.
Likewise:

Likewise, it is said elsewhere:
"Having restrained the mind, that which is signless (alakṣaṇa) should be observed.
By this, the yogi becomes an observer who is devoted to reality."
He who daily and incessantly cultivates the supreme reality— which is non-dual,
peerless, adamantine, and stainless— attains a body that is like a shadow.
In the assembly, however, the Blessed One said:
"This is the most wonderful commitment (*samaya*) of the vajras of body, speech, and mind."
He is eternally to be protected by the holders of the vajra for the sake of all Buddhas.
Whoever protects this commitment, possessing the great splendor of Vajrasattva and having the nature of passion in body, speech, and mind, becomes a Buddha at that very moment.
Elsewhere it is said: "The first is the invocation of Vajra;
the second is that which has entered the vital breath (prāṇa) in the face of Vajra."
This third [chapter] is indeed the non-emission of the glorious bodhicitta,
and it is the great vow of virtue.
That which a monk guards for the sake of the infinite,
and that which a lustful man seeks for the sake of pleasure—
between these two, the jewel of non-dual yoga [is found].
He who grasps it has entered into imperishability.
Without attachment to women there is no happiness of liberation; without attachment to women there is no suffering from the fire of worldly existence.
Therefore, with a wise intellect and a well-discerning mind, [one should act].
May the disciples grasp whatever appears [to them].
From wood comes sacrificial oblation; water even from the moonstone; ghee from curd; iron from ore;
and unimpaired pleasure from union with the female womb.
Let those who are worthy take it up through the application of appropriate means.
Sometimes, due to the power of meditation, the glorious bodhicitta may fall uncontrolled into the center of the lotus;
having recognized this, one should employ a mudrā of perfectly pure mind.
Then, one should grasp it with one's own mouth in the center of that lotus.
For the mind, situated within the lotus of the impure mudrā, is destroyed by the deceptive grasp of the nameless [ignorance].
For the glorious minister [drank] that pure nectar which destroys death, for the sake of savoring it;
thus it is said.
The mind is not stained by passion, nor is it freed from stain by dispassion;
having made passion and non-passion equal, the accomplishment of the mudrā arises.
"Mind arises as the nature of wisdom, and likewise as the form of means;
through the nature of wisdom and means, pure consciousness is born.
Thus it was stated by the venerable Kuddālīpāda in the *Advayasiddhi*.
Through the differentiation of all cognitions, there is the conceptualization of non-duality and duality;
this is called the great secret of wisdom and means, to be accomplished through the single flavor.
The mind is said to take on the forms of both defects and virtues;
the thorough realization of that [mind] is supreme knowledge, by virtue of its waveless nature.
The subterranean pill, the sword, the yakṣiṇī, the sandals, the jar, the mercury, and the divine collyrium— these are accomplished by themselves and not otherwise.
Through the application of the terms of conventional teaching, the Buddha is conceptualized as non-dual;
yet in his ultimate, inconceivable nature, there is neither a Buddha nor even non-duality.
The wise person should strive with effort to exhaust the latent impressions (vāsanā);
otherwise, purity will not be attained even in tens of millions of countless eons.
Wisdom is established as the enjoyment of the nature of selflessness, while means is that which generates existence; thus it was taught by Bhadrapāda.
During the eclipses of the moon and sun, through the application of the wisdom-vajra,
when non-dual gnosis has dissolved, Buddhahood is attained in this very life.
The venerable Indrabhūti, together with Lakṣmī;
Vilāsavajra, Guḍarī, and the most compassionate Padmācārya.
Following Dharmapāda, Bhadrapāda arrived in succession;
they were of one intention regarding the supreme non-dual knowledge.
And the thirteenth is renowned as the auspicious ground, Vajradharī;
it arises in the form of a triangle and is known as the Dharmodaya.
Filled with the moon, the sun, and water, she is the embodiment of wisdom, intensely radiant;
through bliss and supreme bliss, she brings about the attainment of Buddhahood.
"This yoga was taught to me by Bhadrapāda in a playful manner;
it is the meditative absorption named *Amṛta*, which is the truth, the absolute truth, and not otherwise.

Thus it is stated in the *Ghaṇṭāpādīya-pañcakrama*. Now, the sequence of the *maṇipūraka* is described: by means of the procedure for the great yoga of the *samayamudrā*, when the bodhicitta has reached the jewel at the tip of the *vajra*, whatever bliss arises—one having correctly perceived that through the guru’s instruction and stabilized it—when brought to a state of identity with that, it certainly produces the state of a Vajradhara in this very life, provided one does not waver.

The second stage also, by means of the mudrā called *kara*, recognizes— as before— the bodhicitta that has attained stability; having become of an eternal nature, its ultimate essence being non-conceptual, it accomplishes the state of Vajradhara.

The third stage also [is as follows]: the state of being a Vajradhara, which has attained perfect stability arising from the mental seal (mānasīmudrā) and the Dharma-seal (dharmamudrā) produced by the recollection of what was previously experienced, brings about [the realization of] Vajradharahood.

The fourth stage is called Maṇipūraka. It is said that the mind—pervasive, free of focal points, possessing the nature of all that is stable and moving, embraced by the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) of emptiness which pervades the three realms, and having an inconceivable nature—having arisen through the grace of the Guru and been stabilized, accomplishes the state of Mahāvajradhara and generates the bliss of all Mahāmudrās.
In the *Guhyāvalī*, Daṇḍīpāda has also said:

"Therein, first, having abandoned the pleasure of women at the intermediate moment of the final stage of passion (*virama*), he who is absorbed in that [state] takes up another, the immutable pleasure (*akṣarasukha*)."
That wise and illustrious one, skilled in the art of sealing with camphor by the command of his guru,
does not fall into delusion, his mind reeling from drinking the wine of his own bliss.
If that very same absolute bliss which was previously attained through union with a beloved is now [attained], what further need is there for the attainment of the Seal of Emptiness?
Here resides consciousness; other than that object of external pleasure, there arises from it some other, supreme Śambhu of innate bliss.
Even in a deity who has performed noble deeds in a blessed abode,
there is a certain power that makes manifest what is placed within;
for a man who is a lord of yoga but resembles a beast lacks such power.
Even a deity, though fashioned from soft yet heavy stone, is hollow within.
The moment arising between the two joys is so extremely subtle that it cannot be perceived;
how then can one mentally realize the state [of the union] through the conjunction of the vajra and the lotus at that time?
Therefore, virtuous people diligently resort to the bliss of the syllable alone; by remaining there for a long time with a concentrated mind, they again grasp the ultimate reality.
The knowledge of reality is twofold: that which is expressible with words and that which is inexpressible;
one proceeds from limb to limb, while the other does not proceed beyond this.
Of these two, that which prevails through their constant non-contradiction in unity is [the true state].
This very one is self-established, the teacher of the higher path that shatters the lower paths.
Likewise, in the Yamāntaka Tantra:
"Then, having seen the street of banners, one should prepare milk there."
By means of the practice of [consuming] milk, even Mahāmudrā is accomplished.
Thus it was also stated by Saraha in his *Prabandha*:
"If one does not fall away from the objects of the senses, that itself is the state of Buddhahood."
Just as there is no attainment of a tree without seeds and sprouts, so too,
alas, this worldly familiarity seeks after that very thing— thinking "liberation is distinct from existence"— in its pursuit of delusion.

If [the Self] is seen as not being the ground [of phenomena], then how can this distinction exist— namely, that the three worlds are beyond "this-ness" (idantā) and are characterized by the darkness of grasping at existence, non-existence, and both?
Whatever one hears, sees, smells, tastes, perceives, or touches— know that, by virtue of its profundity and magnanimity, it possesses the radiance of Samantabhadra.
Know that these very women are indeed those [goddesses], along with the hosts of glorious Vajra-women; know that these very men are indeed those glorious Maṇḍala-beings.
Know that this very one is the great body of the glorious Vajrin himself.
Thus, this drama of the world is established as being luminous by nature.

"The Teacher," "the disciple," likewise "suffering" and "pleasure," "birth" and "destruction," likewise "action" and its "fruit"— what need is there for further elaboration? His [power] is indeed the three worlds themselves.
This is the playful sport of the Blessed One, the Lord of the Gods.
And so it is said in the *Devendraparipṛcchā-tantra*:
"The letter E is the mother, while the letter VA is traditionally known as the father."
The drop (bindu) therein is yoga; that yoga is the supreme syllable (paramākṣara).
The letter *e* is indeed Prajñā, and the letter *va* is the Lord of Rapture (*suratādhipa*);
the *bindu* is the Unstruck (*anāhata*) reality, and from it all other syllables are born.
He who, knowing reality, understands the two syllables of the seal of the Dharma,
shall become a turner of the wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings.
The person who constantly recites these two syllables without understanding them is an outsider to the Buddha's teachings, like a wealthy man devoid of enjoyment.
Likewise: Having pressed the vajra upon the lotus, one should not emit the bodhicitta;
in order to make the three worlds consist of that [bodhicitta], one must not transgress the physician’s word.
At the emergence of the dyad, one should meditate upon the Hero who resembles the moon in the sky, who pervades the universe,
who has come into being, and who bestows the state of non-duality.
Likewise:
"By means of the yoga of the non-emission of semen, one should meditate on the supreme syllable;
when the support has undergone emission, there is detachment of that which is supported."
In this book, the venerable Āryadeva has clearly stated the instruction on meditative cultivation (*bhāvanopadeśa*).

In a secluded garden, free from the presence of *śrāvakas* and others, having first taken the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) as one's object of focus, one should generate oneself in the form of Vajrasattva through the process of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*). Then, having tasted the three kinds of sensory objects, such as form and so forth, one subsequently prepares all food according to the ritual of purification and other methods. Recollecting the internal hearth (*adhyātmakuṇḍa*), one generates the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) thinking, "I am offering my own form into the mouth of the Samādhisattva as a three-pointed fire," and then consumes it.

Thereupon, it is digested with ease and becomes an elixir (*rasāyana*). Having thus satisfied the body-vajra, one should visualize any woman whatsoever in the form of one's own consort (*svābhā-prajñā*), her limbs adorned with every ornament; she is beautiful with the undulating waves of her three folds [of skin], her waist exceedingly slender, her deep and expansive navel region concealed by a line of hair; her broad hips and heavy buttocks are firm, and she moves with a graceful, tender gait, her face smiling, and she stands upon one's lap with a gentle gaze, through the passion of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Then, generating a firm sense of self-identity, thinking "I shall accomplish the great siddhi," one performs embracing, kissing, sucking, grasping the breasts, thrilling, striking, biting and scratching with the teeth and nails, massaging, the sounds of *śītkāra*, and the cooing of the cuckoo and the humming of the bee, as well as the stimulation of the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth. Through the joy produced by the actions of the needle, the elbow, and so on, and by the friction of the moving pearl necklaces, bracelets, rings, armlets, anklets, vajras, and lotuses, through the union of wisdom and means, [one proceeds] from the nature of the aggregates and so forth, beginning from the heads of all the Tathāgatas...

The seventy-two thousand channels, having melted into the form of liquid *ali* and *kāli* like the flow of a waterfall, proceed through the sequence of passion (*rāga*), dispassion (*virāga*), and intermediate passion (*madhyarāga*). Thereby, they cause one to realize within oneself the essential nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth. Thus, the yogi who has practiced the glorious samādhi of great bliss and attained excellence should, right there in the maṇḍala of the assembly, bring sentient beings to maturity through both subduing and favoring them.

In this manner, repeatedly entering the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and repeatedly arising from it, he enjoys the five sense-qualities (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) in the form of the five Tathāgatas so that his mind does not wither. Then, the non-conceptualizing great yogin, in order to demonstrate the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as being his own self, purifies what is censured in the world and, remaining in a secluded place, partakes [of them].

And thus, there is no binding of mudrās, no maṇḍala, no caitya, no recitation of books, no bodily mortification, and one does not bow before images made of cloth, wood, or stone; nor does one pay regard to the lunar days, constellations, or auspicious moments. All this one accomplishes through the internal self alone.
The practitioner of firm resolve should always wander for alms in the forest.
Terrified by fear, they offer food consecrated by divine mantras.
One whose nature is the three vajras may transgress [these bounds], yet the indestructible vajra remains;
whether it be a goddess, a woman, a great yakṣī, an asurī, or even a human woman.
"Having attained the vow of knowledge (*vidyāvrata*), one should perform that which is served by the wisdom of the three vajras.

Thus, having cast aside worldly meditation and abandoned mental kingship, always weeping with a mind like that of Sadāprarudita, and sporting with the yoginīs, he—just like King Indrabhūti—transforms his physical body, becomes a vajra-body, and together with his inner circle of queens, vanishes from sight. Endowed with the qualities of the eightfold sovereign powers, he travels from buddha-field to buddha-field, as it is said in the *Mūlasūtra*:
Being served at ease with all the enjoyments of the gods,
one should worship one's own self through union with one's own presiding deity.
The *Sarvadevasamāgama-tantra* also says:
"Through the union of the two organs, that rite is to be meditated upon within;
the mind of joy of the Sage, when perfected, is known as great bliss (*mahāsukha*)."

Thus, constantly enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure while seeking the five types of knowledge, one who possesses passion will quickly become a Buddha, a lord of the great ocean of wisdom. However, for one who, due to incapacity or by personal preference, does not practice the *vidyā-vrata*, he should cultivate [the realization] through the attainment of the *jñānamudrā*. This is now introduced: in a place such as a mountain that is favorable to the mind, one should accomplish the rites for the *yakṣiṇīs*, *kiṅkaras*, and so forth, for the sake of obtaining food and drink. Or else, from a superior practitioner...

36) Or, having prepared even a single bowl of food for the Mahāsattva, first the practitioner, recollecting the suffering of beginningless saṃsāra and desiring the bliss of nirvāṇa, must become one who has renounced all attachments; he must perceive even sovereignty over a kingdom as suffering. Second, he must abandon the notion of possession regarding even things as small as a sesame seed. Third, with reference to ultimate truth, he must become indifferent toward both body and life.
Fourth, as it is said in the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*:

Therefore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires this samādhi and wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must be one who is not attached to body or life. Likewise, he should not seek the eight worldly accomplishments, because they cause distraction and lead to regression.
And so it is said in the *Guhyasiddhi*:
"The knower of reality should always avoid ritual applications and the like in their true nature;
except for the ego-identification with Vajrasattva, he should not perform anything else."
Even the application [of practice] would not be understood by those established in the pure reality,
as long as it is not scrutinized through the application of the state of selflessness.
For one who stands upon the state of selflessness and is endowed with divine means,
whatever arises from conceptual construction is accomplished without deliberation.
Through the power of the yoga of meditative cultivation, all that constitutes the characteristics of accomplishment, whatever it may be, manifests of its own accord in a single instant. Thus.

Therefore, having cast aside external women and relying on the audacity [of thinking], "I shall very swiftly accomplish the state of the Great Vajra through union with the Wisdom-Mudrā residing within the heart," one should meditate alone according to the Guru’s instruction. Thus, with diligence, one must avoid causes that obstruct virtue; for the sake of pacifying distraction, one should practice the conduct of Bhusuku according to this sequence: *bhu* means having eaten; *su* means having slept; *ku* means having gone to a hut—therein one should remember only that [reality]. Or, one should act according to the vow of a madman, as it is said in the *Guhyasiddhi*:
Assuming the form of a madman, remaining silent and composed,
he should wander like a *piśāca* through the yoga of his own presiding deity.
For the purpose of wandering for alms, the observer of the vow should not collect a bowl;
rather, he should take up a discarded vessel from the street, such as a potsherd or a broken bowl.
One should wander for alms in that very place; having obtained food, one should eat it while exerting oneself;
and having eaten it there, being satisfied, one should discard it right there.
Then he should wear a loincloth that is torn and tattered;
or else, having become naked, he may wander about as he pleases.
It is also said in the *Sarvarahasyatantra*:
"But those who have arisen from selflessness, who are born of non-dual gnosis,
and who are free from the desirable and the undesirable— they do not bow down to anything at all."
Such is the detailed explanation. For silence quickly illuminates reality; therefore, one should practice it with diligent effort.
As it is said in the *Mahāmāyottaratantra*:
"Within six months, by virtue of necessarily becoming mute,
that great yogi, attended by the yoginīs, blazes forth."
Even when there is no gain of alms, the yogin should maintain only a state of mental well-being (*saumanasya*) and cultivate reality (*tattvabhāvanā*).
As it is said in the *Buddhakapālatantra*:
"For the yogin who has renounced everything and is devoted to reality does not give rise to the notion of non-existence (*śūnyatābhāva*)," and so forth, in detail.
When the hero, having abandoned worldly stability, acts without conceptual construction, he performs all activities; the Buddhas behold him always.
One who has severed all doubts should move powerfully according to reason in every respect;
when the yogi becomes free from appearances, then prosperity rains down upon him.
For those possessed of every sin and firmly established in the veil of delusion,
unfailing success is attained within six months through the practice of the madman’s vow.
One shall see all the Buddhas face to face and be fulfilled by all desires;
there is neither exhaustion nor diminution, and one’s body arises with a lifespan according to one's own wish.
Whether walking, standing, or sitting, one should always proceed with profound words;
for yogins, this is the constant characteristic arising from skill in the luminous consciousness.
By this very yoga, the jewel of the mind becomes firm;
and the Buddhas, established in awakening, bestow their empowerment.
Thus, having become firmly established therein, one who is devoted to cultivation should practice meditation.
As long as the mind of the wise one, whose mind is composed, does not become weary, he should wander about; afterwards, he may act according to his own inclination.
Cultivating vast awakening with eyes slightly opened,
he may laugh, talk, stand still, or move about; yet,
with his mind intent on meditation, he ensures that no weariness arises.
Thus, for the mantra-practitioner who is endowed with such meditative concentration and free from conceptual construction,
the unsurpassed state is accomplished by transcending the limits of time.

In this way, for one who practices according to the distinctions of inferior, middling, or superior capacity, and in accordance with their age— for a fortnight, a month, or up to six months— the signs of the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā arise.
In this regard, the sign (nimitta) is as follows:
it is a subtle form, light to the touch, and indeed all-pervasive; it is luminous, stable, characterized by mastery, and extends to the limit of one's desires. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, regarding the signs of dreams, it is said in the *Śrī Guhyasamāja Mahāyoga Tantra*:
"One sees the Buddha of radiant splendor, who has attained the supreme gnosis of awakening;
and one quickly perceives oneself as the Buddha’s saṃbhogakāya."
And he sees it being constantly worshipped by the great beings of the three realms,
as well as by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
He constantly beholds the worshiped one, whose radiance is equal to great gnosis—
the Great Vidyā of Vajrasattva, the Great Renown of Vajrasattva.
One of great resolve beholds one’s own form as a secret vajra in a dream;
the great Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajradharas prostrate before them.
Such dreams as these shall be seen, bestowing the accomplishments of body, speech, and mind.
One who sees a beautiful celestial maiden adorned with every ornament,
or a boy or a girl, attains accomplishment.
He certainly beholds the field of all the Buddhas of the ten directions;
with his mind and self focused in vision, he bestows the delightful treasury of Dharma—
the body that has entered the wheel of Dharma, surrounded by all sentient beings.
One sees [this] in the state of yoga as being established in the vajra of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, he speaks of the internal signs:
first, the appearance of a mirage; second, resembling smoke;
third, the form of fireflies; and fourth, a blazing lamp.
"But the fifth is Sadāloka, with the radiance of a cloudless sky.

Thus, one should understand that the *karmamudrās* are categorized as weak, middling, and intense according to the threefold division of means (*upāya*). Furthermore, all [practitioners], whether ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) or those established in the state of non-retrogression (*avaivarttika*), [should practice] at a shrine (*caitya*).

Such is the tradition. Thus, through practice that is gradual, according to one's inclination, performed with devotion, continuously, and for a long period of time, there is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā;
but not by means of mere knowledge alone. And so it has been said by the venerable teacher Śākyamitra: "Just as fire residing within wood does not emerge without friction."
Without such practice, enlightenment will not arise even in this very life.
Likewise, it has been said by Kambalāmbarapāda:
"Dharma that is not cultivated does not lead to the attainment of Dharma."
How much more so does water, when drunk, destroy [thirst]? What need is there to mention seeing or hearing it?
If anything at all is to be cultivated here, what is the use of speaking of this group [of things]?
Even a horn might be seen upon the heads of rabbits and horses;
even a frog might appear radiant with a mass of matted hair, grey with dust,
wearing a white sacred thread and carrying a water-pot slung over its shoulder.
As it is said in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:

"By gradually following the sequence of the stages (*bhūmi*), the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), and their objects, and by contemplating the triple world as one's own mind through the conviction that it is like an illusion, they attain the illusion-like samādhi. Merely by entering into the non-appearance of one's own mind, they reach the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-vihāra*), free from the connection with activities such as arising, and [attain] the body of the Tathāgata which conforms to the vajra-image of samādhi..."

"Mahāmati, Bodhisattvas shall attain the body of the Tathāgata—which is adorned with powers, superknowledges, mastery, compassion, and mercy; which arises from all Buddha-fields and the abodes of the heterodox; which is devoid of mind, intellect, and consciousness; and which is preceded by the transformation of the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

Therefore, Mahāmati, Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas who seek to attain conformity with the body of the Tathāgata must become free from the conceptual proliferation of discrimination regarding the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, mind, causes, conditions, activity, conjunction, arising, duration, and destruction."
Kambalāmbarapāda also stated in the *Adhyātmasādhana*:
"They say the gross [form] consists of sound, and likewise the subtle consists of mind;
that which is devoid of thought is the supreme state of yogins."
And so it is said in the *Śrīhevajra*:
"The syllable Śrī is non-dual gnosis; He is the emptiness of causes and so forth."
The array devoid of the letter "ru" is not established anywhere as "ka."
And so it is said in the *Saptaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā*:
"That which is the non-apprehension of all phenomena is the perfection of wisdom."
Likewise:
"The revolution of the basis, which is free from all conceptual constructions,
and this supramundane gnosis— this is the Dharmakāya of the Great Sage."
That is the vajra; he is Vajrasattva, the Buddha, the unsurpassed awakening.
Among all yogas and super-yogas, this yoga is supreme.
This is the foremost yoga for determining the compendium of reality and for the great samaya-reality in the glorious *Vajrābhiṣeka*.
In the great samaya of Mahāmāyā, in the glorious assembly of Buddhas,
in the supreme primordial Great Tantra, the glorious Vajra-Mahāsukha.
And in the *Śrī-Samāja-mahātantra*, this unsurpassed yogin is described by Cittavajra as the accomplisher of all siddhis;
those sons of the Victors who have transcended error herein [attain this].
They become, before long, the Victors, the teachers of the three worlds. Thus it is said.
The *Śrīsaṃvara* also says:
"With hands, feet, and so forth everywhere; with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere;
possessing ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading everything."
This is the natural body (*svābhāvikakāya*), the non-duality of emptiness and compassion;
it is known as the "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) and in some places as the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*).
Because the aggregates and so forth abide here by virtue of the unobscured nature (*nirāvaraṇadharma*),
this entire maṇḍala is characterized by the relationship between the support and the supported.

Therefore, by this gradual process, that practitioner of reality (tattvayogin), because he consists of the removal of all superimpositions, becomes identical with the nature of the fivefold awakening through the removal of each respective superimposition; and being of the nature of all the deities of the maṇḍala, having become their very self, and through the state of single fusion (*ekalolībhāva*)—due to the non-consideration of all distinctions—he, though free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), fulfills all the hopes of all sentient beings through the teaching of the Dharma and other means, by means of inexpressibly inexpressible millions of Bodhisattvas, Tathāgatas, mantras, and mudrās, for as long as saṃsāra endures.

He brings them to fulfillment; then he comes to abide in the stage of the highest-of-the-high degrees. Because he accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings through non-conceptuality, he is unshakable by the winds of all discursive thoughts, like a wish-fulfilling gem. Abiding thus, he fulfills the hopes of sentient beings without exception.
Illuminating this very point, it is said in the *Śrī Guhyasamāja Mahāyoga Tantra*:
"All the Tathāgatas proclaim:
'O Vajra! O Vajra! O teaching of the Vajra!'"
Where there is no body, speech, or mind, there form is manifested. Thus it is said.
And so it is said in the *Hastikakṣya-sūtra*:
"In this, there is neither suchness nor a Tathāgata;
for form alone is seen throughout the entire world."
The venerable Śāntideva has also said:
"Just as a snake-charmer, having empowered a pillar, destroys it;
even long after that [pillar] has perished, he can still neutralize poisons and the like."

Just as the wish-fulfilling gem and the wish-granting tree fulfill desires according to one's wishes, so too does the form of the Victor appear through the power of those to be trained and his own previous vows.
Thus— in all tantras, this supreme reality of mantra has been taught by the Protectors, who conform to the inclinations of those to be trained, as something to be inferred.
For those who are incapable of knowing this reality of mantra, the meditation on origination through the sequence of the moon, sun, and so forth has been prescribed. Thus it is said.
For one who meditates in this way, there is no transgression, nor even the occasion for a transgression.
Thus it has been said:
"The intention of Bodhisattvas is either virtuous or non-virtuous."
Everything becomes auspicious for those whose minds are under control.
Therefore, whatever is done for the benefit of others by those whose very nature is compassion—
all that activity is proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones as "teaching."
Likewise:
"Even while desiring the Mother of all the Buddhas, the All-pervading One... he is not defiled at all. Buddhahood is accomplished for that wise one who is free from conceptual construction."
Likewise: "Those beings who have committed the immediate transgressions, even those who have performed great evils;
those beings who take life and those who delight in false speech."
Those who subsist on excrement and urine as food are indeed fit for the practice of sādhana.

As it is said in the *Karmāvaraṇapratiprasrabdhi-sūtra*: Suppose there was a certain monk who had fallen into a defeat (*pārājika*) through unchaste conduct and the killing of a human being. Later, with a distressed mind and a burning heart, like one driven mad, he wandered from monastery to monastery and from village to village, even going into the streets and other public places, proclaiming that sin before all people. Crying out "I am robbed! I am robbed! again and again, he raised a great lamentation; yet, by the power of confessing that sin, he did not descend further [into hell], but rather thinned out that karma. For him, [the result] was not obtained... (p. 45)

When one whose mind is thus tormented is taught the profound Dharma in such a manner by a certain Bodhisattva who has attained superknowledge (*abhijñā*), that person completely uproots all that evil and, through the penetration of the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*), becomes an attainer of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*). Therefore, it should be understood that this resolute belief in the profound Dharma (*gambhīradharmādhimokṣa*) dispels all transgressions and purifies all karma. As it is said in the *Tathāgataguhyakośasūtra*:

Kāśyapa, if one were to deprive of life one who is both his father and a pratyekabuddha, this is the foremost of acts of taking life. This is the foremost of acts of taking what is not given: namely, the theft of property belonging to the Three Jewels. This is the foremost of sexual misconducts: namely, if one were to violate a woman who is both his mother and an arhat. This is the foremost of lies: namely, to bring a false accusation against a Tathāgata. This is the foremost of divisive speech: namely, to cause a schism in the Saṅgha.

This is the foremost of harsh words: namely, the reviling of the noble ones. This is the foremost of frivolous chatter: namely, the distraction of those who desire the Dharma. This is the foremost of covetousness: namely, the intent to seize the gains of those who have entered the right path and are practicing correctly. This is the foremost of ill-will: namely, the undertaking of an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*). This is the foremost of wrong views: namely, an utterly profound and dense state of view.

These ten unwholesome paths of action are all greatly blameworthy. Kāśyapa, if some single sentient being were to be possessed of these ten unwholesome paths of action, which are thus blameworthy, yet were to enter into the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma concerning causes and conditions—[realizing] that herein there is no self, nor sentient being, nor life-principle, nor person who acts or experiences [the result]—then, because of this state of non-action...

He penetrates the conditioned nature, the non-defiled nature, the illusory nature, and the intrinsic luminosity of all phenomena; he has faith in and resolves upon all phenomena as being primordially pure. I do not say that such a being will go to the states of woe. There is no accumulation of afflictions, for afflictions arise, break apart, and dissolve. They arise through the conjunction of a collection of conditions; as soon as they have arisen, they cease.

“Blessed One, the very destruction of the arising of the thought [of awakening] is itself the destruction of all afflictions. For one who has such conviction, there is never any transgression, nor any occasion for transgression; it is impossible and out of the question that a transgression should remain in the unobstructed state. Such a situation does not exist. [The Blessed One replied: “Even for those whose minds are inconceivable, non-action is not prescribed. However, those who do not know reality and are devoid of merit are ruined. He said:
“Thus, those who do not know reality rely merely upon what they have heard.”
They do not perform meritorious deeds; they are ruined within the teaching of the Buddha.

By this sequence, through the enjoyment of all objects without exception, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā arises; this is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru by way of a compendium of well-spoken instructions.
Thus ends the Compendium of Sublime Sayings.
